title: Jamie Dimon Urges US Not to Punish India Over Russian Oil Purchases
excerpt: The JPMorgan chief told CNBC-TV18 that tariffs on Russian crude buyers would hurt India and world oil markets, urging Washington to finish a trade deal instead.
body:
• JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told CNBC-TV18 the United States should "sit down" and avoid punishing India over its purchases of Russian oil.
  • Dimon said he was "not sure" Washington should impose "any kind of tariffs on the oil," warning against damage to India and global oil markets.
  • The remarks come as a 2026 US law authorizes tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian energy.
  • Dimon also urged New Delhi and Washington to finish their stalled trade agreement, calling the two countries natural partners.

What Dimon said

Speaking to CNBC-TV18's Prashant Nair around JPMorgan's India investor conference, Dimon addressed the escalating pressure on India over its Russian crude imports head-on. "I think hopefully America will sit down and understand all those issues and, you know, not end up punishing India and the world oil markets while doing what we need to do to combat Russia," he said. He added that he was "not sure" the United States should put "any kind of tariffs on the oil."

"I think hopefully America will sit down and understand all those issues and, you know, not end up punishing India and the world oil markets while doing what we need to do to combat Russia."

— Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase CEO, to CNBC-TV18

Dimon made a refining argument that policymakers often skip: Indian refineries are configured for specific crude grades, and substitutes may not run properly in those units. Punishing the buyer, in his framing, does not just squeeze Russia; it disrupts physical supply chains that cannot be rewired overnight.

The tariff threat hanging over India

The context is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which gives President Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian energy. Trump signed a related sanctions bill into law last week, and India is squarely in the frame: Russia's share of Indian crude imports hit record territory this summer, topping 50 percent in July by some tallies, as Gulf barrels disappeared amid disruptions around Hormuz and the Red Sea.

India imports roughly 5 million barrels per day, and the stakes go beyond oil. Current US tariffs on Indian goods already stand at 50 percent; analysts cited by CNBC-TV18 note the energy tariffs would stack on top, potentially taking the total burden toward 150 percent. That would make Indian exports sharply costlier in the American market. Estimates put the direct energy cost of replacing discounted Russian barrels at $3-5 billion a year, before counting the hit to exports and the current account.

A wider warning on the war and the relationship

Dimon, who has long praised India's reforms — he has called Aadhaar an "unbelievable achievement" — used the interview to argue that Washington should be pulling New Delhi closer, not pushing it away. He cautioned the Russia-Ukraine war "could easily" drag on another five years, said it was getting "harder and harder for India to remain non-aligned," and urged both governments to sit down and complete a trade deal. "India and the U.S. have strong business links and should work towards greater stability in their relationship," he said.

The wide-ranging conversation also touched the AI investment boom — hyperscaler spending potentially rising from $300 billion last year toward $1 trillion next — the Federal Reserve's 2 percent inflation target, which he defended, and US immigration reform, where he backed action on DACA, merit-based immigration and a path to citizenship for law-abiding undocumented immigrants.

What it means for the diaspora

For Indian Americans, the tariff fight is not abstract. Indian exporters — from textiles to engineering goods — face the prospect of their products becoming uncompetitive in the US market, with knock-on effects for diaspora-owned businesses on both sides. Energy-driven inflation in India would also squeeze remittance value and travel costs. Dimon's intervention matters because it frames the issue the way markets see it: as a choice between pressuring Moscow and destabilizing one of America's most important economic partnerships.
